why_angle: The cited rivals give maker specs only. StormWatts says it has not tested these products hands-on, and EnergySage says it did not test them. Neither has a measured idle draw, and idle draw is what separates these kits in a multi-day outage: about 85 W for the Jackery 5000 Plus (HOBOTECH), about 21 W for BLUETTI's RV5 (Zelpio) and about 10 W for the Anker S5000 (pv magazine). This page puts those readings beside each kit's shipping state, price per Wh and refill hours.

page.after:
What the differences mean

Dealectric does not test units. Prices and shipping states come from the stores on 2026-11-17. Idle and capacity readings come from the reviewers named beside each figure. Here is how each figure is worked out:

  • Price per Wh = link price ÷ battery Wh. RV Kit + 4 × 100W: $4,084.05 ÷ 5,120 Wh = $0.80.
  • Full-sun hours to refill = battery Wh ÷ panel watts at rated output. RV Kit + 4 × 100W: 5,120 ÷ 400 = 12.8 h. Panels deliver less than their rating (pv magazine saw a 680 W peak from 800 W of Anker panels, 85%), so expect longer in practice.
  • Idle loss per day = measured idle watts × 24 h. Jackery 5000 Plus: 85 W × 24 = 2,040 Wh, about 40% of its 5,040 Wh. RV5: 21 W × 24 = 504 Wh, about 10% of 5,120 Wh.
  • Against the same parts (BLUETTI store, 2026-11-17): the RV Kit + 4 × 100W costs $716 less than the RV kit plus four PV100 FX panels bought separately. The Apex 200 + B300K kit costs $198 less than its parts, and the Apex 300 + B300K + 2 × 350 W kit costs $101 more than its parts.

Where the line was drawn: a battery of 4,000–6,000 Wh (5 kWh ± 20%), sold with its panels as one listing. Left out: BLUETTI Apex 200 + B500K (7,680 Wh), Apex 300 + B500K (7,884.8 Wh), Apex 300 + 2 × B300K (8,294.4 Wh) and the Elite 400 kits (3,840 Wh). EcoFlow's DELTA Pro 3 (4,096 Wh) is left out because a search of EcoFlow's US store on 2026-11-17 returned no DELTA Pro 3 panel kit. The EcoFlow TITAN 5000 Plus is a whole-home battery with no panel-kit listing.

Idle draw: what the inverter burns with nothing plugged in

A switched-on inverter draws power even when no appliance runs. On a 5 kWh battery through a multi-day outage, that standing loss decides how many days you get. These are the readings reviewers measured:

At HOBOTECH's 85 W, the Jackery's inverter alone would empty a full battery in 5,040 ÷ 85 = 59 h, about 2.5 days. At Zelpio's 21 W the RV5 would take 5,120 ÷ 21 = 244 h, about 10 days. Usable energy on a full discharge is close: HOBOTECH measured 4,450 Wh from the Jackery at 120 V (88%), Zelpio 4,300 Wh from the RV5 kit (84%, the better of two cycles), and pv magazine 4.87 kWh from the S5000 (97%, as reported by the app). The gap between these kits in an outage is the idle draw, so on the Jackery, turn AC output off whenever nothing is running.

The RV kit is not a box you plug lamps into. Zelpio found no built-in outlets on the RV5: its 120 V AC output is hardwired into the RV's distribution panel. BLUETTI ships it with wood screws, a drilling template and a distribution-panel wiring pack, and its FAQ says most RV owners can install it with basic DIY skills. Each solar input takes 12–50 V (RV5 manual), so the 100 W panels are wired in parallel rather than in a high-voltage string.

Not recommended

BLUETTI 5kWh RV Kit + 2 × 100W. 200 W of panels needs 5,120 ÷ 200 = 25.6 h of rated full sun to refill, which takes several clear days in practice. The 4 × 100W kit costs $285 more ($4,084.05 − $3,799.05) and halves the refill time.

BLUETTI Apex 300 + B300K kits. On 2026-11-17 the 2 × 350 W kit cost $101 more than the same parts bought separately at BLUETTI, and the 2 × 200 W and 500 W versions cost $102 and $150 more. All three dispatch in late January 2027. If you want this system, buy the parts separately.
